principles.title: How I work
principles.subtitle: Looking back through my notes, three things kept repeating

rootCause.title: Fix the cause, not the symptom
rootCause.description: When something breaks in production I don't stop at putting out the fire. I read library source and logs until the cause is certain, and I follow problems that started outside the frontend to wherever they came from.

typeLevel.title: Make the same failure impossible
typeLevel.description: Recurring problems get structural fixes rather than individual patches. When two things must not overlap, I make overlapping unrepresentable; when a state is invalid, I make it impossible to express rather than checking for it.

enforceWithTools.title: Leave rules as tools, not documents
enforceWithTools.description: What I find myself repeating in code review moves into a lint rule or automation. A document can go unread — lint has to pass.

architecture.title: Problems from production, and how I solved them
architecture.subtitle: Less about what I built, more about why it's shaped that way and what I chose not to do

trpc-migration.title: Mock data kept drifting between test environments
trpc-migration.summary: Consolidated an API layer that had split across environments into one entry point
trpc-migration.problem: Every new feature meant imitating the same API two different ways — Storybook used module mocking because MSW can't intercept server actions, and E2E used something else. One API with two imitations meant the mock data silently drifted, and tests could pass while the real thing was broken.
trpc-migration.decision: I routed API requests through a single point and layered a type-safe layer on top. Each endpoint keeps its request, schema, and mock data together in one folder, so the schema and its mock always live side by side. Middleware wraps in logging → error → auth order, so logging observes the final transformed error.

rejected.0: Keep the existing approach with a stronger shared wrapper — the split-mocking problem would remain untouched
rejected.1: Call the backend directly from middleware — token handling scatters again

trpc-migration.result: Storybook, E2E, and local development now share the same mocks, so they can no longer drift. New domains extend the same structure.

reactive-session.title: Valid sessions were being logged out
reactive-session.summary: Replaced client-side expiry estimation with reacting to the server's response
reactive-session.problem: Users who were properly logged in were getting signed out. The client calculated token expiry itself and refreshed preemptively, but with the frontend and backend each judging expiry separately, the two drifted apart. In a service where real money moves, losing your session mid-contract means losing the work you were doing.
reactive-session.decision: The frontend stopped estimating expiry and started reacting to 401s. The key is splitting the outcome three ways: refreshed, rejected, and transient. Mistaking a 5xx or network error for expiry turns a brief outage into a site-wide logout. Concurrent 401s collapse into a single refresh, and the refresh call itself goes through a separate client so it can't recurse.

rejected.0: Refresh the cached expiry more often — clock skew remains and request volume grows
rejected.1: Put refresh on the server — refresh state is per-user, so the server would need a shared structure that breaks across instances

reactive-session.result: Expiry judgment moved entirely to the server, eliminating frontend/backend mismatch. Auth-dependent queries were also centralized into a shared hook, removing requests that fired before authentication and got rejected.

overlay-coordinator.title: Required modals got buried behind other overlays
overlay-coordinator.summary: Replaced independently-opening overlays with a priority that picks exactly one
overlay-coordinator.problem: Several overlays appeared automatically based on conditions, each managing its own open state. Collisions were prevented only by z-index numbers, so the policy for who wins existed nowhere in the code. Modals the user had to see kept ending up behind other overlays.
overlay-coordinator.decision: One slot on screen, with array order as priority. The crucial part is returning a single active overlay — instead of managing overlap, the overlapping state became unrepresentable. Registration accepts only a state-derived value and imperative calls are blocked, so there's no second copy of the state to fall out of sync.

rejected.0: Fold in user-triggered overlays — built, then rolled back. Those are opened by the user directly, so they never collide; the machinery only added complexity
rejected.1: Unify the backdrop dim — built, then rolled back. That element isn't a visual effect but the host of scroll locking, so removing it unlocks scrolling

overlay-coordinator.result: Each overlay now only declares its intent to appear, and priority decides the single active one. Both rolled-back extensions are documented with their reasons, so the next person doesn't walk the same path again.

vrt-infra.title: Every deploy meant checking things by hand
vrt-infra.summary: Test executions grew 4×, while CI time dropped 30%
vrt-infra.problem: Changing one line meant re-checking unrelated pages. Financial flows have too many conditions to verify manually. Adopting E2E created the opposite problem: a fixed shard count wasted runners when tests were few and starved them when tests grew.
vrt-infra.decision: The pipeline counts the tests to be run and derives the shard count each time, so neither time nor resources tip too far. The build runs once and every shard reuses the output. Tests split into three layers — user behavior, implementation, and shared setup — so a failure immediately tells you whether the scenario or the implementation broke.

rejected.0: Raise the worker count — measurement showed billed time is the sum of job durations, so it didn't drop. It also caused mock contamination and flaky failures, so I reverted
rejected.1: Gate CI on screenshot comparison — font rendering differs between local and CI. A tight threshold breaks on environment noise; a loose one misses real changes. I scoped it to a review aid instead

vrt-infra.result: Test executions grew 4× while total CI time fell 30%, cutting CI time per test by roughly 80%. I later measured that sharding reduces wall-clock time but increases billed time, and trimmed duplicate triggers and concurrency groups to cut billed time per merge roughly in half.

backend.title: Fixed a sort bug in the backend repo
backend.description: I followed a list-ordering anomaly found on the frontend into the backend. With only one sort key, rows sharing that value got reordered between pages — some duplicated, others silently disappeared. I added the primary key as a tie-breaker, along with a test that fails if the tie-breaker is removed.

review.title: Code review and team standards
review.description: I approve and comment rather than block — if it isn't worth stopping the flow, I don't stop it. What I find myself repeating in reviews gets moved into a lint rule or a document, so I don't have to say it twice.

writing.title: Technical writing
writing.description: I published our E2E adoption experience on the company engineering blog. Architecture decisions live in documents — including the ones we rolled back, with the reasoning intact. I only write when a problem I hit connects to a principle.

closing.title: Build it, roll it back, write it down
closing.description: Several things were finished and then deliberately discarded. I record what I rolled back so the next person doesn't have to walk the whole path again to learn the same thing.

paragraphs:
A frontend developer in my second year working with React and TypeScript,
 currently operating and improving an early-settlement financial service.
I believe every piece of development should serve business value, and I work to look after both UX and DX in service of that.

allra.title: Allra
allra.subtitle: Allra Fintech
allra.description:
An [B]early-settlement financial service[/B] that lets e-commerce sellers receive revenue ahead of their payout date. I joined just as the Next.js migration finished, and took on correcting logic that had been dropped or mistranslated in the move while hardening the service for production.

Because the product moves real money, [B]ISMS certification was the largest undertaking[/B]. I redesigned session and token handling to meet its requirements and closed the paths where credentials were leaking into logs and browser autofill. Alongside that, I traced production failures beyond the frontend to their real causes and improved the deployment and testing environment so the whole team could verify changes faster and more safely.

categories.title: ISMS certification — redesigned authentication and session architecture

details.text: Moved session handling from a client that [B]computed token expiry itself and refreshed preemptively[/B] to one that [B]reissues in reaction to backend 401s[/B] — consolidating the source of expiry truth on the server and eliminating client/server disagreement about when a session ended
[B]Centralized auth-gated queries behind a shared hook[/B], [B]eliminating the wasted network calls[/B] fired by off-screen components before authentication and rejected on arrival
Improved the error-handling logic so error types are classified correctly, and removed the logic that was blocking error propagation, closing a path that [B]bypassed auth gating[/B]

categories.title: Modeled settlement application state and consolidated duplicated implementations

details.text: On the form where sellers enter how much to draw forward per marketplace, defined each row's state as a [B]6-member discriminated union[/B] (loading, fetch-failed, ineligible, invalid input, empty, submittable), [B]pinning the cases the UI must handle into the type system[/B]

Each child component computed [B]available limit, settlement fee, and early-seller subsidy[/B] in its own useEffect, accumulating branches with every policy addition — moved computation into a Provider so children only render

Because [B]subsidy depletes sequentially across marketplaces[/B], one row's input changes another row's fee — resolved with a [B]two-pass calculation pipeline[/B]: the first pass determines each row's state, the second deducts subsidy [B]in fee-rate order[/B] across submittable rows only, making the calculation order explicit
[B]Extracted the fee, limit, and subsidy logic into pure functions[/B] guarded by [B]unit tests[/B], so changes to settlement policy surface regressions in tests first

Attaching the [B]business registration, ID, and bankbook documents sellers submit for a settlement contract was implemented separately in four flows[/B], losing confirmation results — unified into [B]a shared state machine[/B], removing the retry loop caused by a dependency cycle between hooks: measured before/after deployment, [B]upload retries per user fell 58% and contract completion time dropped 84%[/B]

Condition-triggered overlays [B]stacked on each other and buried required modals[/B] — unified behind a coordinator where each declares only its intent to appear and [B]priority decides the single active one[/B]

To verify complex financial flows, structured E2E tests into [B]three layers — Spec (user behavior), Flow (implementation), and Sequence (shared preconditions)[/B] — with API mocking and fixtures reproducing edge cases automatically ([L:https://allrafintech.co.kr/blog/137]company engineering blog[/L])

CI time scaled linearly as tests grew — I framed it as a tradeoff where [B]a fixed shard count either wastes runner resources on empty shards when tests are few, or runs short on shards and stretches runtime as tests grow[/B]. Designed [B]a matrix that counts the tests to run and derives the shard count dynamically on every run[/B], [B]keeping time and resource use in balance rather than optimizing one at the other's expense[/B]: as test executions grew 4x, total CI time still fell 30%, cutting [B]CI time per test by ~80%[/B]

Later verified by measurement that [B]splitting into more shards cuts wall-clock time but actually increases billed time[/B] — billing is the sum of job durations, so every split adds cost. [B]Consolidated concurrency groups, removed duplicate triggers, and cleaned up flaky test logic[/B] to [B]cut billed time per merge by ~52%[/B]
[B]Automated the repetitive test-writing work with an AI skill[/B] and consolidated the supporting docs into a single source so the team works the same way

After leaving Vercel to cut costs, designers and PMs had to [B]run Storybook locally[/B] to review UI — [B]proposed and built per-branch preview deployments[/B] so they could [B]review from a URL alone[/B]

digitalFinance.title: Digital Finance
digitalFinance.subtitle: Samil PwC AC
digitalFinance.description:
A [B]unified portal[/B] for managing the various services used inside Samil. I joined a project already underway, owned the frontend, and saw it through to production.

In the accounting domain, [B]clearing internal security review was a precondition for shipping[/B]. Replacing a build tool that had stopped receiving security updates and an editor that violated policy was the core work, and I added a server-state layer that replaced caching and synchronization previously handled by hand.

categories.title: Build system migration and structural cleanup

details.text: Migrated the build system to [B]Vite[/B] after CRA was deprecated and ruled out by internal security policy, cutting [B]bundle size by 58.3%[/B]
Replaced an editor that violated the internal [B]CSP policy[/B] with react-quill-new, [B]building a custom image-resize module[/B] to close the gap
[B]Introduced Tanstack Query to split server state[/B] out of a Zustand store that held both, fixing screen inconsistencies caused by duplicate requests and stale data

documentAi.title: Document AI
documentAi.subtitle: Samil PwC AC
documentAi.description:
A [B]document analysis solution[/B] where AI analyzes reports. I owned the frontend end to end, from design through deployment.

Displaying and finely controlling many PDFs at once was the core feature, so I [B]built the viewer myself[/B] and solved the slowdown that came with document count through virtualization and parallel processing. Since the product was installed directly into client on-premises environments, reducing deployment size mattered just as much.

details.text: Built a [B]custom PDF.js Viewer[/B] to meet the core requirement of fine-grained control over multiple PDFs, applying [B]Web Worker + react-window virtualization[/B] to cut [B]initial render time by 67%[/B]
On-premises installation at client sites made the large image a deployment bottleneck — applied [B]standalone mode + multi-stage build[/B], [B]cutting image size by 91.36%[/B]
Introduced dynamic-import code splitting, [B]cutting bundle size by 73.5%[/B]

samilDevKit.title: SamilDevKit Design System
samilDevKit.subtitle: Samil PwC AC
samilDevKit.description:
A [B]component- and token-based design system[/B] used across PwC products in-house, released as v1 together with the whole frontend team.

At that early stage the structural foundation mattered most. I established a type-safe styling pattern built on clsx and cva, and moved JS-state-driven animations to CSS transforms for reflow-free 60fps.

allraAdmin.title: Allra Admin
allraAdmin.subtitle: Allra Fintech
allraAdmin.description:
The [B]internal admin[/B] used to operate the settlement service, living in a monorepo shared by several projects. I migrated the legacy PHP v1 to Next.js and [B]built the authentication and audit layer required for ISMS certification[/B].

In a financial admin a misbehaving API reaches real data immediately, so a safe way to verify work mattered as much as the features themselves. I proposed and built a mocking environment that reproduces every scenario without depending on the live API.

details.text: Calling the real API made failure and edge conditions hard to produce on demand. A mocking layer that lets responses be shaped freely allowed us to [B]reproduce errors, latency, and insufficient-permission paths[/B] alongside the happy path — organized so the team uses it the same way.
Designed and implemented [B]role-based authorization and token handling[/B] against ISMS requirements, together with an audit layer that keeps access traceable.
